Honesty

Why it works this way

These are decisions, not shortcomings. Each one narrows what procoder does, each one was measured before it was taken, and none of them costs a finding the tool would otherwise have reported. They lived on what it misses for five editions, where they read as apologies. They are rationale, and they belong here.

The test that split the two pages: a decision we made deliberately is not a limitation. Where a deliberate decision does cost the reader a finding — an escaper trusted by name, a cap on how much the hook prints — it stays on what it misses, under accepted trade-offs, with what it buys stated next to what it costs. Everything on this page fails silently in the safe direction, or does not fail at all.

The ratchet: what a fingerprint is made of

hooks/checks/baseline.js fingerprints each finding from its rule id, its file path, the normalized text of the statement the finding sits in — extended forward while a bracket or an operator is still open — and an occurrence ordinal. The line number is deliberately excluded.

Every property below was verified against a baselined finding. What the choice buys is stability under edits that changed nothing: reindenting a file, or moving a suppressed line up or down, does not resurrect a suppressed finding, and a re-wrapping formatter no longer breaks it — statementAt reads the whole open construct and drops a comma added before a closer, so db.query(x) and the prettier-wrapped form of the same call fingerprint alike. Copy-pasting a suppressed line does not ride in for free either: the occurrence ordinal gives each copy its own identity, so only the first is suppressed.

What it costs is in one direction only — a finding is re-reported, never missed:

EditWhat happens
Moving code between files The path is part of the fingerprint, so a relocated violation is a brand-new finding rather than a tracked move. Verified: baseline a.js, move the function verbatim into b.js, and verify exits 1 with the finding listed as new. Tracking moves would mean matching content across a whole tree, and a ratchet that guesses at identity is a ratchet that silently forgives.
Editing line 1 of a file with a file-level finding obvious/nesting-depth is reported at line 1, so its fingerprint is over whatever the file's first line says. Add a copyright header or an import and the accepted finding returns. Verified end to end.

The baseline itself no longer grows without end. procoder baseline prunes an entry whose finding is fixed or gone and says how many it dropped — verified: three accepted entries, fix every finding in the tree, re-run, and the file reports 0 accepted findings, 3 pruned — fixed or gone. An entry carrying the string unknown for its date is stamped with today's on the next write, exactly as verify --aging says it will be — verified: a hand-edited unknown entry came back as {"id":"safe/dynamic-eval","path":"a.js","added":"2026-08-17"}.

One thing about added is worth saying plainly: it is data the user owns. It is hand-editable, nothing signs it, nothing cross-checks it against git, and exactly one thing reads it — --aging. A date edited to last week resets the clock on a year-old suppression, silently. That is the same trust the config file already has.

The baseline format is versioned, and old baselines are not migrated

BASELINE_VERSION in hooks/checks/baseline.js is 4. It moved from 3 when entries began recording their rule, path and date, and earlier fingerprints cannot be reconstructed from what a v3 file holds. A stale-version file therefore loads as an empty accepted set, never a partial one — a partial migration would suppress an arbitrary subset and call it a ratchet. Verified against a hand-edited v1 file:

  • procoder verify exits 2, distinct from the 1 used for "the ratchet grew", and says the baseline is the wrong format — CI does not blame the user for a backlog they did not add.
  • procoder check prints the same stderr notice but still reports every finding in the repository, because nothing is suppressed. The exit code is the ordinary one.
  • procoder baseline always overwrites with a current-version file, so running it is the fix in both cases.

The failure direction is more findings, never fewer, which is why this is a decision and not a defect.

The TOML parser is a documented subset

hooks/checks/toml.js exists to read .procoder.toml and nothing else. A general TOML parser would be a dependency, and rung 1 says a new dependency is a new trust boundary. What it supports: [tables], [dotted.tables], dotted keys (a.b = 1), basic strings with escapes, literal strings, int, float, bool, and arrays — single-line or spanning several lines, with trailing commas and comments inside the array. Verified working: s = "a\"b" loads a"b, s = 'C:\src\' loads the backslashes as written, paths = ["a, b", "c"] yields two entries, and so do nested arrays, mixed-type arrays, CRLF and a BOM.

What makes the subset safe rather than lossy is that everything the parser cannot read exactly is warned about on stderr, with file and line, and the key is left unset — which falls back to the stricter default. Verified refusals, each warned and none guessed at: inline tables (t = {a=1}, including inside an array), dates and times, hexadecimal (0x1f), underscored (1_000), exponent (1e6), inf, +1, bare unquoted words, quoted keys ("a b" = 1), multi-line strings, arrays of tables ([[x]]), unknown escapes, unterminated strings, and an array that never closes.

A duplicate key is refused in both directions rather than resolved: x = 1 then x = 2 warns .procoder.toml:2: duplicate key, both values ignored: x and leaves x unset, rather than taking the last. A repeated [table] header warns duplicate table header, section ignored. Verified end to end: a .procoder.toml with paths written twice under [exclude] excludes nothing and says so. A duplicate says two things and TOML permits neither, so keeping either one would be a guess.

One construct still loads a value nobody wrote, and because it does so in silence it is the one row of this section that stayed on what it misses: a scalar and a table of the same name.

Deliberate narrowings from performance work

Every long-line path in the engine was made linear, and each rewrite was proven behaviour-identical by differential runs. The ceilings that survived are real and are listed here rather than left in the source. Each one announces itself when it bites — which is what separates these from the three that cut silently, and those three are on what it misses as accepted trade-offs.

NarrowingWhereEffect, measured
20 findings per line hooks/checks/run.js Overflow is reported as its own finding (true/findings-suppressed) naming the count, never silently dropped. Verified: a line of 3,000 minified try{f()}catch(e){} blocks reports 20 findings plus line 1: 2980 further findings suppressed (cap 20 per line). No honest line reaches 20.
1 MB per-file skip hooks/checks/config.js, applied in run.js Down from 4 MB to 2 MB, and again to 1 MB. The language pack is the one stage that cannot be abandoned part-way — everything after it is deadline-driven — so the size of what it is handed is the only lever on its cost, and the taint rebuild roughly doubled the ts pack's constant. 1 MB of ordinary source costs the worst pack ~400 ms of the 2,000 ms budget here, which still finishes on a host three times slower; 2 MB did not. Verified: a file of exactly 1,048,576 bytes is checked; at 1,048,577 procoder check prints skipped exact.js (too-large) — not checked. on stderr, and procoder verify over the same tree exits 2.
[limits] max_file_bytes, downward only hooks/checks/config.js A project may lower the cap, never raise it. max_file_bytes = 999999999 warns is above the measured ceiling 1048576 — using 1048576; 0, -5, "big" and true each warn must be a positive number of bytes, ignored and fall back to 1 MB. Set it too low to admit any file and procoder verify names every file it could not check and exits 2 rather than declaring a ratchet over a run that read nothing.
2 s budget, and what it cuts hooks/checks/run.js Checks after the deadline are skipped. The language pack runs before the project's linter, and the linter is paid a share of what is left on the clock (0.6, floor 100 ms) rather than a precomputed split, so the total is under budget by arithmetic on any host rather than by a constant measured on one. Worst case at a 3× slowdown went from 1,797 ms to 1,448 ms of 2,000 ms, and holds to 6×. What the deadline cuts is loud on both channels: a true/budget-exhausted finding appended after the per-file cap, so five SAFE findings cannot push it out, plus a stderr line naming the stage. The universal pack (rung 1) runs first of all and can never be the stage that is cut.

The budget is uniform: the parent puts it in the worker's payload and passes it on the sequential path too, so a file scanned inside a worker runs at the same 2,000 ms. Verified — hooks/checks/scan.js exports SCAN_BUDGET_MS at 2,000 and no SLICE_BUDGET_MS at all. The 200-character SPAN_MAX that used to bound the universal pack is gone.

The self-scan's own arithmetic

tests/dogfood.test.js derives its file list from git ls-files, so a file is inside the gate the day it lands. Both of its hold-out lists — HELD_OUT and PENDING — are empty, and both are checked for still earning their place: the test fails if a HELD_OUT path matches no tracked file or has gone clean.

Measured today over 212 tracked files, procoder check . reports 0 findings and exits 0, having skipped 18 of them and said so on stderr for every one:

  • 9 by [exclude] paths in .procoder.toml, one line per pattern with its count: 7 tests/fixtures/*/dirty.*, and one each for .opencode/command/rot.md and .openclaw/commands/rot.md. The dirty fixtures exist to be scanned by the tests rather than by the scan, and a line marker in one would change the input the test reads. The other two carry exactly one finding each, named in .procoder.toml next to the entry, with the source fix named too.
  • 9 by two .procoderignore files: 5 under docs/superpowers/ — 1,500-line planning documents for work already executed, quoting rule ids by the hundred, verified at 56 findings under --no-ignore and every one of them meta-text — and 4 examples/*/before.*, files that violate a rung on purpose, verified at 10 findings under --no-ignore and still checked on every test run through that flag.

So 194 files are actually read, and README.md publishes those three numbers; tests/dogfood.test.js asserts them against the scan's own output, so the paragraph fails the build rather than going quietly out of date. The repository root also carries a .procoderignore for .claude/ and .superpowers/; both are untracked agent scratch, so the count it skips is whatever the machine happens to be holding and is not a reproducible number.

This list was 46 files until the staleness rules existed to judge it. Of the 32 generated rule files then excluded on the "it is generated" argument, 30 held nothing back at all — they are rendered from skills/procoder/SKILL.md, which is itself in the gate, so the markers that keep the source clean render into them too. They are gated now. The remaining two are one false positive, not a category.

Every exclusion is re-judged, and where that stops

unusedPathExclusions in hooks/checks/config.js reports a configured path exclusion three ways — its path no longer exists, it matches no file in the tree, or every file it covers is clean — under plain verify, failing the build only under --unused-exclusions, which is the contract unusedRuleExclusions has always had. Verified in a throwaway repository: paths = ["keep/", "**/*.gen.ts"] with keep/ holding one clean file and no .gen.ts anywhere names both and exits non-zero under the flag. unusedIgnorePatterns judges a .procoderignore the same way and on the same contract, one pattern at a time, naming file, line and the pattern as written.

The two tree-wide rules are decided only when the run's targets covered the whole repository — "this glob matches nothing" is a claim about the tree, and a verify over one file has not seen it — so a partial run says nothing, deliberately. Three more limits on the same instrument are deliberate too. There is no "the path is gone" rule for an ignore file: a literal path there is a fence around a location, and such a location is legitimately absent from a fresh clone, as this repository's own .claude/ and .superpowers/ lines are in CI. A pattern covering only untracked files is never judged, because content the repository does not own cannot go clean in any sense procoder can verify — and where git ls-files cannot answer, no ignore pattern is judged at all. And a negated pattern (!keep.js) is never judged, because "this exception stopped mattering" is not a claim about coverage lost. All three of this repository's own ignore files are silent under these rules, by rule rather than by exemption.

--no-ignore does not reach [exclude] paths

The flag answers "why is this file not being checked?" by turning off every .procoderignore for the run, and nothing else. [exclude] paths is the project-wide contract, written once at the root and reviewable in one place, and it carries the built-in node_modules/, vendor/, dist/ defaults — so a flag that reached it would be a back door into node_modules, not a diagnostic. Verified: with [exclude] paths = ["sub/"], an injected safe/sql-injection in sub/x.js is silent under procoder check . and under procoder check --no-ignore . alike. It is not silent about itself: both runs print 2 files skipped by [exclude] paths "sub/" in .procoder.toml, and naming the file on the command line prints skipped sub/x.js ([exclude] paths "sub/" in .procoder.toml) rather than answering a direct question with silence.

.claude/ is deliberately not in procoder's built-in defaults, so a user starting a scan at their repository root sees findings from whatever their agent tooling leaves there until they write an ignore file of their own. .claude/ also holds hand-written hooks and scripts, and a default exclusion would un-gate those silently for everybody.

Config keys

.procoder.toml's supported keys are documented in Configuration and in README.md, and are deliberately not duplicated into the limitations record — a key documented in two places is a key that will be wrong in one of them. tests/docs-drift.test.js fails the build when the engine reads a key the reference does not mention, and when the reference documents a key the engine no longer reads.

Every measurement on this page was produced by running the tool at 0.2.0, not read off a previous edition. Where a number here and a number in docs/known-limitations.md disagree, the markdown is the record and this page is stale.

No fonts, no analytics, no scripts. This page makes no external request.
